Testimony Against LD 2165 An Act to Change Supervisory Authority over the Capitol
Police
Prepared and presented by Kevin Anderson, Executive Director MSLEA
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfuss, and distinguished members of the Criminal
Justice and Public Safety Committee.
My name is Kevin Anderson, I am here as the Executive Director of the Maine State Law
Enforcement Association. In this role I represent over 400 State Law Enforcement Officers to include Game Wardens, Marine Patrol Officers, Forest Rangers and Capitol Police Officers in
collective bargaining and labor related matters.
Prior to this I was a Game Warden For 12 `/2 years in the Augusta District and a Game Warden
Investigator for a little over I3 years. I served as cadre at the 14*" and 15`h Maine Criminal
Justice Academy Basic Law Enforcement Training Program. In those roles, I had the pleasure to work with members of the Maine State Police daily. I say this to make it clear that none of my
testimony today is meant to in any way indicate that I believe that Maine State Police Ofiicers do not deserve the compensation and recognition that they receive. They are some of the finest law
enforcement officers in this state.
That being said, I am here to testify against LD 2165. The title of this bill is misleading and the
changes go far beyond the stated title of the bill.
The Bureau of Capitol Police has been in existence in one form or another since 1968.
Within the past two years, both the Maine State Police and the Capitol Police engaged in the reclassification process with the State. That process is initiated with the submission of a FJA-1, Functional Job Analysis, a document that provides a detailed work description. The reclassification results provide employees in those positions with a pay grade which results in a placement on the State pay scale.
The most recent pay scales indicated that State Police Troopers make between $12 to $15 dollars more an hour than Capitol Police Officers in the same place on the step progression.
State Police Detectives make between $6-7 more dollars and hour than a Capitol Police
Detective.
State Police Sergeants make $7 to 8 more an hour.
State Police Lieutenants make $10-12 more an hour.
A state Police Lt makes more an hour than the Chief of the Capitol Police.
These numbers do not include standby pay which in some classifications amounts to tens of
thousands of dollars a year. A benefit Capitol Police Officers do not receive.
1

These pay parity gaps may in fact be larger whereas they do not reflect pay increases awarded
from recent contract negotiations for State Police Officers.
These numbers do not take into account that fact that Maine State Police Officers all get issued a
take home vehicle and most Capitol Police Officers do not. Additionally, State Police Ofiicers
are assigned to a more expensive retirement plan than Capitol Police Officers.
Numbers provided by the Commissioner of Public Safety indicate that the replacement of a Capitol Police Officer with a State Police Trooper will cost the taxpayers an additional $100,000 in pay and benefits per position vs. the cost of a Capitol Police Officer performing the same job.
In a press release issued but the Department of Public Safety it was stated that this change was being made with the future in mind and that "Threats against our legislatures and properties
continue to grow." That may be true and the Capitol Police Department has grown in recognition
of this trend. The Capitol Police has been provided funding by this legislator to add a Detective
position, a bomb dog and handler, and a new secure entry kiosk with screeners and a Capitol
Police Officer in the Cross Building next door. The Capitol Police recently sent a newly hired
officer through the MCJA Basic Law Enforcement Training Program, also known as the blue pin
or full-time law enforcement academy. This is the first time in Capitol Police history that I am
aware of for this Bureau that dates back to 1968. The current law does not require it, but the prior Chief recognized the increased demands on the Capitol Police Officers. All Oflicers hired over the past several years at the Bureau of Capitol Police are experienced full time law enforcement
officers who have held previous law enforcement jobs as Police Chiefs, Police Lieutenants,
police Detectives and Police Officers. They bring life and law enforcement experience to the
Capitol Police.
The role of Capitol Police Officer is probably one the most forward-facing law enforcement positions in the state. Capitol Police staff have daily contact with hundreds of people on a daily basis when legislature is in session and must exercise a high degree of patience and professionalism as they provide safety for the legislature and the thousands of people that visit the capitol on a weekly basis to testify on frequently emotionally charged issues. They have done this exceptionally and there has been no indication that they are not up for this task. There have been no known complaints indicating that they have not been keeping up with the demands.
This bill indicates that the replacement of Capitol Police Ofiicers will "occur through attrition" as is also stated in an email sent by the Commissioner to Capitol Police Staff If that is true, then
this transition could in fact take place over 25 or more years based upon the minimum number of
years the newest officer would have to complete to retire at the full retirement benefit.
The statement released by Public Safety indicates that this change "will improve resource allocation, operational efficiency, and crisis response" . There is currently no specific issues with any of these. I have asked the Capitol Police Officers that I represent if there has been any issues
2

in communication, crisis response, or operational efficiency and I wasn't surprised to hear that there was none.
The Commissioner recognizes the impact of this change in his email to staff where he states, "This is a major change that will impact you in both a personal and professional manner." That is a true fact and an understatement.
This bill will cause chaos, confusion and uncertainty within the Capitol Police. This change will
mean that employees within the Capitol Police could potentially be operating under three separate contracts, which means three separate sets of work rules. State Police Troopers, Sergeants, and Detectives are represented by the Maine State Troopers Association, State Police
Lts,,Capitol Police Lts and Capitol Police Sergeants are represented by the Maine State Law Enforcement Supervisors Association or FOP and the Capitol Police Detectives and Capitol Police Officers are represented by MSLEA.
During impact bargaining held with the Department of Public Safety it was revealed that Troopers assigned to the Capitol Police role will wear the State Trooper uniform and Capitol Police Officers will wear the current uniform.
Currently the Department had not agreed to address the huge pay parity issue this bill will if it is enacted and begins to be implemented.
Capitol Police Officers will lose the opportunity to promote within the Capitol Police unless they want to apply to the Maine State Police, participate in the hiring process to be a Maine State Trooper and then if hired, complete State Police Recruit Training. Then and only then at some
point when there is an opening, the Capitol Police may apply for a position with the planned
Capitol Police Troop.
In closing, I didn't want to come here and ask that you vote ought not to pass on this bill without
offering a solution to this problem.
What I ask this committee to do is change the law to require that all newly hired Capitol Police Officers moving forward, must be certified full time law enforcement officers or upon hire must complete the full-time law enforcement academy at MCJA.
I would ask this committee either keep the State Police Lieutenant as the replacement for the Capitol Police Chief and leave the other positions as they are or task the Commissioner with
finding a new Police Chief to lead this Bureau into the future. Many of you on this committee
participated in hearings in regards to the Fire Marshals Office two years ago. If I had told you two years ago the Fire Marshals Office was going to be on an upward trajectory tmder the current leadership of Chief Fire Marshal Sean Esler, you probably wouldn't have believed me, but it's true. Chief Esler has completely changed the path and atmosphere at the Fire Marshals Office.
With that being said, I am confident that the Commissioner can find a new Capitol Police Chief who can lead these men and women into the future while addressing all the concerns of the
3

Commissioner in a more fiscally responsible manner than having the State Police take over the Capitol Police role, while also avoiding the chaos and confusion that will come with this proposed plan.
The price tag associated with this takeover would be enough to double the number of Capitol
Police Officers under the current Capitol Police structure.
Thank you for your time and I will be happy to answer any questions you have at this time.

Testimony of Senate President Mattie Daughtry in support of LD 2165, "An Act to Change Supervisory Authority over the Capitol Police" Before the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety
March 4, 2026

Good afternoon, Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety, my name is Mattie Daughtry. I serve as President of the Maine Senate and proudly represent Senate District 23, including Brunswick, Freeport, Harpswell, Pownal, Chebeague Island, and part of Yarmouth. I am testifying in favor of LD 2165, "An Act to Change Supervisory Authority over the Capitol Police."

As a legislator, I know firsthand how important our safety infrastructure is here in the Capitol complex. We are a citizen legislature, working in collaboration with our constituencies to serve and uplift our state together. Our facilities are public buildings, easily accessible to the public because that is who we are and who we are here to serve, the people of Maine.

The world is changing. The risks associated with public service have evolved significantly in recent years. While our tradition of accessibility and public participation is a powerful example of democracy in action, the very openness that defines our Legislature can also expose us to real risks. Members of the Legislature are experiencing new and evolving security concerns, reflecting the changing nature of public service in an increasingly polarized and digitally connected world. According to the Capitol Police, threats against Maine lawmakers have more than doubled since 2023.i These threats have targeted legislators across the political spectrum. We have seen these threats firsthand, including a bomb threat this session that locked down the building and derailed legislative work.ii

Our Capitol Police officers have responded to these challenges with dedication and kindness. They are trusted members of this community. This bill is not a reflection of dissatisfaction with their service. Rather, it recognizes that as the threat environment changes, our structural framework must evolve as well.

LD 2165 strengthens coordination by aligning the Capitol Police within the Maine State Police supervisory structure. It provides a clearer chain of command and expanded access to training, facilities, and operational resources -- while retaining the officers who know this building and its people so well. Leveraging existing state infrastructure and expertise is also a responsible use of taxpayer resources, allowing us to strengthen security without duplicating systems or creating unnecessary bureaucracy.

Our Constitution establishes three separate, co-equal branches of government. As your committee considers this modernization of our safety infrastructure, I urge you to do so in a way that reflects

that structure. While I support this bill and the professionalization opportunities it advances, I also believe the Legislature must retain an appropriate role in overseeing the safety systems that protect our own branch of government. As we strengthen the Capitol Police's structure and training through alignment with the State Police, we should also ensure that clear lines of accountability and input remain with the Legislative branch. The safety and security of our legislative complex directly affects how safely and effectively this great institution can function every day. If we want to preserve a citizen legislature that remains open, accessible, and reflective of our state, we must ensure that its safety systems are modern, coordinated, and responsive to today's realities. Strengthening the structure that supports our Capitol Police is ultimately about protecting the institution itself AND the people who serve here. Public safety is a fundamental responsibility of our democracy, and ensuring the safety of this institution allows us to continue doing the people's work without distraction or disruption. Thank you for your consideration and I urge you to support LD 2165.

TESTIMONY OF SPEAICER RYAN D. FECTEAU PRESENTING LD 2165, An
Act to Change Supervisory Authority over the Capitol Police

Good morning Senator Beebee-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and esteemed members
of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee. I am House Speaker Ryan Fecteau, and I have the privilege of representing my hometown of Biddeford.
I am here today to present LD 2165, An Act to Change Supervisory Authority over the Capitol Police, a govern0r's bill which I am happy to sponsor.
LD 2165 is an important step in merging the Capitol Police and Maine State Police, a
transition that will help improve operational efficiency, manage resource allocation, and enhance crisis response capacity. Enhancing the partnership between Maine State Police and Capitol Police will strengthen existing information-sharing and create a unified
command in light of increased demand for services.
Specifically, this bill will transfer supervision of the Capitol Police to the Chief of the State Police. It will reclassify the Capitol Police Chiefs position to that of a State Police
Lieutenant, who would serve as the commanding officer of the Capitol Police. It allows for
a gradual transition through the natural process of attrition, so that over time as Capitol officers leave their jobs, they will be replaced by a state police officer position.
The current environment is more polarized than ever, and in turn, the volume of threats directed at public officials is on the rise. I know we all feel the impact of this.. Over the past four years, the Capitol Police have seen a 180% increase in threat complaints. These complaints were largely against members of the legislature, with no regard for political affiliation or family situation. The Capitol Police have done a great job responding to the heightened demand, and I believe these changes will help us improve coordination even further, and capitalize on all of our existing resources.
Every public servant and elected official deserves to feel safe. I encourage the committee
to pass this bill to help achieve this goal. I also understand that DPS has been in conversation with bargaining units and is putting forward a friendly amendment as a result of those ongoing discussions, which I will let them detail in their testimony. I am happy to answer any questions, but will mostly defer to experts from the Department who
will testify after me. Thank you for your time and consideration.

An Act to Change Supervisory Authority over the Capital Police.
Sponsored by Senate President Daughtry and Speaker Fecteau Committee on Criminal Justic and Public Safety
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and honorable members of the Committee on Criminal
Justice and Public Safety:
My name is Major Tyler Stevenson, and I am providing testimony on behalf of the Maine State Police and the
Maine Department of Public Safety in support of LD 2165, "An Act to Change Supervisory Authority over the Capitol
Police."
This bill would transfer supervision of the Capitol Police to the Chief of the State Police and reclassify the
Capitol Police Chief's position to that of a State Police Lieutenant, who would serve as the commanding officer of the
Capitol Police. Through natural attrition, as Capitol Police officers vacate their positions, those positions would be reclassified to State Trooper positions if funds are available.
On December 15, 2025, under the direction of Department of Public Safety Commissioner Michael Sauschuck,
the State Police assigned a Lieutenant to supervise the day-to-day activities of the Capitol Police. This decision
followed months of careful consideration and evaluation of all options, with the goal of providing the best possible
policing and security services. The women and men of the Capitol Police are professionals who take great pride in their work, and I have been impressed with my interactions with them and my observations of their performance.
The benefits of placing the Capitol Police under the umbrella of the State Police are numerous and positive for both agencies and for the Capitol Complex. Passage of this bill would result in improved resource allocation, greater operational efficiency, and enhanced crisis response capabilities. The State Police have access to greater personnel resources, advanced technology, investigative support, and specialized units, including the Tactical Team, crowd
management, K-9, bomb squad, and Major Crimes Units.
Merging Maine State Police standards with the Capitol Police would ensure uniform and consistent law enforcement standards across the Capitol Complex. Capitol Police officers would gain direct access to State Police
reporting systems, technology, fleet resources, policies, and command structure. The Maine State Police also maintain

The current political threat environment is higher and more dynamic than at any point this century, and it continues to evolve. As it stands, the State Police Executive Protection Unit (EPU) and the Capitol Police work well together, but they are separate organizations operating under different executive administrations. If the Maine State Police were charged with providing police and security services to the Capitol Complex, it would be natural for EPU to fall under the command of the same entity. Benefits of this alignment include improved communication, enhanced information and intelligence sharing, and consistent training, policies, and equipment.
This bill would create a critical force multiplier for the Capitol Complex. Capitol Police and EPU are currently being stretched by today's threat environment, and having troopers assigned to the Capitol Complex who possess the training, education, and experience to supplement EPU staff as needed, will be essential in addressing both current
and future security concerns. A single chain of command would promote clear communication, a shared understanding of mission, and a direct flow of information from the ground level to executive leadership regarding
both Capitol and gubernatorial security. In the past, these missions have at times involved duplicative objectives and
strategies.
The State Police have experienced significant success in recruitment and retention over the past four years.
Since 2021, we have hired 108 troopers, and we believe we can bring this success to the Capitol Police, which has historically struggled to fill its ranks. This structure would also create a more robust command framework, including
the Maine State Police Major of Support Services, Lieutenant Colonel, and Colonel, under the authority of the Commissioner of the Maine Department of Public Safety.
Over the past four years, the threat environment has changed dramatically. In 2022, the Capitol Police
received six complaints involving threats to the complex or legislators. That number increased to 23 in 2023, 53 in
2024, and 111 in 2025. This bill represents a necessary and proactive step toward providing the resources necessary to mitigate today's threats and prepare for those of tomorrow.
On behalf of the State Police and the Department of Public Safety, we appreciate your careful consideration of these issues. Thank you for your time and I would be happy to answer any questions at this time.

SUMMARY
This bill transfers the supervision duties of the Chief of the Bureau of Capitol Police Within the Department of Public Safety to the Chief of the State Police and replaces the position of Chief of the Bureau of Capitol Police with a State Police Lieutenant position. The bill provides rule-making
authority regarding security at the capitol area to a designee of the
Commissioner of Public Safety and requires that rules adopted governing security at the legislative offices and other offices within the capitol complex include consultation with both the Commissioner of Public Safety and the Chief of the State Police. The bill also requires that the Chief of the State Police replace a Capitol Police officer position that is vacated with a state police officer position, contingent upon the funding of the reclassification of
that position.
